newsitem.title: NEW ZEALAND: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - March 12.
newsitem.headline: PRESS DIGEST - New Zealand newspapers - March 12.

text.p: THE DOMINION

Nearly three-quarters of the police officers who quit last year received payouts from the Police Employment Rehabilitation Fund, Police Association advocate Greg Fleming said on Tuesday. Fleming said 332 of the 461 officers who resigned received PERF payouts after two doctors had verified that psychological or medical conditions prevented them from doing their job. Page 1.

Labour MP Trevor Mallard was served with a writ for libel for $1.05 million by lawyers acting for NZ First MP Tukoroirangi Morgan on Tuesday. The writ follows the issuing by Mallard of a tape that he said was a recording of a conversation between Aotearoa Television shareholder Eric McPhee and director Morehu McDonald. He said the tape, left anonymously on his desk, included information damaging to Morgan. Page 1.

Deputy Prime Minister and Treasurer Winston Peters will find out on Wednesday whether his late-night scuffle with fellow Coalition member John Banks in Parliament last Wednesday will go before the powerful privileges committee, or whether it will end up with the police. Speaker Doug Kidd bowed on Tuesday to a request for more time by Peters, who said he had not been able to attend to Alliance leader Jim Anderton's complaint about the incident till Monday. Page 2.

The government has deferred a decision on whether to introduce a carbon tax. On Tuesday Environment Minister Simon Upton announced the delay till after an international meeting in December to consider legally binding gas emission targets. Greenpeace climate campaigner Adam Laidlaw criticised the decision, saying a carbon tax would have an almost immediate impact on gas emissions, whereas a global scheme would take years to put in place. Page 2.

The state superannuation scheme would be too costly to continue when the income-tested surcharge was abolished and the impact of the aging population hit home, Prime Minister Jim Bolger said on Tuesday night. He told the New Zealand Investment Conference in Auckland that now New Zealand was moving away from income-tested entitlement to superannuation with the removal of the surcharge, it was clear a "major rethink" was necessary. Page 2.

Prime Minister Jim Bolger has been accused of dodging questions over allegations the Serious Fraud Office canned inquiries into the financial dealings of the Bank of New Zealand in order to "please" a minister. In the House on Tuesday, Labour leader Helen Clark asked Bolger if he was taking steps to assure the public that none of his ministers impeded such an inquiry. Page 2.

Corporate tax rates could be lowered along with personal tax rates within the next three years, Treasurer Winston Peters said on Tuesday. Peters told the New Zealand Investment Conference in Auckland that the Coalition Government's intention was to lower corporate taxes in the long term. Personal tax rates were to have been lowered in July, but the government has deferred the cuts till July next year to soften the inflationary impact of the extra spending promised in the coalition agreement. Page 17.

Shortland Properties has reported a tax-paid profit of $12.3 million for the year to December 31, up 55 percent on the previous year's result of $7.9 million. The result included unrealised revaluations of $16 million. Equity earnings were $700,000. Properties in the portfolio increased a net $3.7 million and operating revenue rose 32 percent to $20.7 million. Page 17.

It was time people stopped deceiving themselves and congratulating themselves about New Zealand's economic circumstances, Labour Party finance spokesman Michael Cullen said on Tuesday. "As an economic miracle, New Zealand now rates somewhere around Lazarus' funeral," he told the investment conference in Auckland. "I believe it is fair to say that the coalition's economic programme is likely to worsen the imbalances and make them harder to address rather than resolve them." Page 17.

ACT leader Richard Prebble predicted on Tuesday that his party would hold the balance of power in Parliament after the next election as voters turned away from NZ First. Politically, New Zealand had moved to the centre-right. Labour and the Alliance between them gained just 37 percent of the vote in the last election, Prebble said in a speech prepared for the investment conference in Auckland. Page 17.

New Zealand's terms of trade continued to weaken in the December quarter, with exports now buying 3.5 percent less than a year ago, deputy government statistician Ian Ewing said on Tuesday. The department's terms of trade index for the December quarter was down 1.5 percent from September and 3.5 percent lower than in the December 1995 quarter. Ewing said the deterioration was due to export prices falling further than import prices. Page 17.

Goodman Fielder has applied for clearance from the Commerce Commission to buy the New Zealand milling and baking operations of Defiance Mills. Commission chairman Alan Bollard said the commission had 10 working days to make a decision, but this could be extended. It would investigate the proposal and decide the relevant markets and how the acquisition, if it went ahead, would affect competition. Page 17.
THE NEW ZEALAND HERALD

New Zealand motorists could face breath tests for cannabis within three years. A British company that makes alcohol sniffers is developing a similar instrument to test for cannabis use, says the head of traffic safety at police national headquarters, Assistant Commissioner Phil Wright. He says it is still about two years away. Asked if police would consider introducing the sniffer, Wright said on Tuesday: "We certainly will if such a device comes available."

The successful bidder for NZI Life is expected to be known by the end of the month. Tenders closed last Friday and Guinness Peat Group, AMP and Prudential are each understood to have lodged bids of around $150 million. The three were invited to bid after a four-week due diligence process. NZI Life was put up for sale by Scottish-based insurance giant General Accident in a move to return to its core business of fire and general insurance.

Sanitarium Health Food Company is looking to innovative new products, such as Fruity Box and Treasure Treats, to maintain growth as it nears the end of its first century business. During the company's first ever media briefing on Tuesday, the New Zealand sales and marketing manager, Jim Richards, said the mature brands, such as Weet-Bix, Skippy Corn Flakes and Ricies, were providing growth. But the biggest growth was coming from the new products.

It is an increasingly uphill struggle for New Zealand to earn its living in the world, according to terms of trade statistics released on Tuesday. The terms of trade index, which measures the quantity of imports that a fixed quantity of export would fund, fell 1.5 percent over the December quarter. The index has been on a declining trend for the past two years and at the end of last year was 3.5 percent lower than in December 1995.

When the Reserve Bank governor Dr Don Brash hands down his quarterly verdict on the economy on Thursday, he is expected to take a less rosy view of the inflation outlook than he did in December. He is faced with a freer-spending government and signs that pressures from wages and the housing market are stronger than he had expected. The December statement was written before details of the coalition agreement were known.
THE PRESS

Canterbury will miss out on work worth an estiamted $600 million over the next 25 years because of the government's purchase of Seasprite helicopters, says the unsuccessful tenderer. Defence Minister Paul East announced on Tuesday the $274 million purchase of four American-made Kaman SH-2G Seasprite naval helicopters and four earlier F models for training and spares. The Kaman contract includes a New Zealand industry programme worth nearly $100 million, but the Ministry of Defence said no details could be released as the contract will still to be negotiated. Page 1.

New Zealand First says it cannot be blamed for encouraging a climate of racial hostility leading to attacks on migrant families, after leader Winston Peters last year called for tighter immigration curbs. In Parliament on Tuesday Opposition MPs attempted to draw a link between Peters's comments and racial-based attacks such as Monday's attack on a Somali family living in Christchurch, the second in a month. Page 1.

New Zealand First MP Tuku Morgan is seeking $1 million of damages from Labour MP Trevor Mallard and two television stations after they aired details of a tape Mallard said raised new questions about the Aotearoa Television affair. Lawyers for Morgan served a writ of defamation on Mallard, Television New Zealand, and TV3 on Tuesday. Labour believes it is the first time in New Zealand, and possibly the Commonwealth, that a sitting MP has taken legal action against another. Page 6.

A leading sharebroker on Tuesday recommended shareholders reduce holdings of New Zealand shares and bonds. Don Turkington, managing director of Cavill White Securities, said the outlook for equities and bonds was "clouded to say the least, and we recommend lower weightings of both". Not all brokers share his view. Some say that New Zealand bonds still offer good investing. Some pin their hopes on a fall in the kiwi dollar to lift export companies, but many are putting clients into overseas shares. Page 25.

Andrew Ott, a client adviser with Forsyth Barr, Christchurch, said on Tuesday of the sharemarket outlook: "There are clouds on the horizon -- there always are. If not you have a euphoric, bullish market. I talk to clients about investing offshore. Banks have been good investments, but no banks are listed in New Zealand while some good ones are listed in Australia. New Zealand is not necessarily a bad place to have money." Page 25.

Tourism Holdings, formerly the Helicopter line, is uncertain about is annual result after reporting a lower first half. The Dunedin-based tourism group on Tuesday announced a bottom-line profit of $4.118 million in the six months ended December 31, down 16 percent on the same period in 1995. The chairman, Murray Valentine, said the group would report a satisfactory result in the third quarter, but forward predictions for the final quarter were uncertain. Page 26.

Defiance Food Industries on Tuesday advised New Zealand shareholders to take no action on a bid from Bunge Foods Queensland until the company's board made a recommendation. Bunge is offering NZ 207 cents for Defiance Food non-redeemable preference shares. The offer is part of Bunge's offer for Defiance's Australian-based parent Defiance Mills announced last week. Also last week it was announced that Goodman Fielder was to buy the New Zealand Milling and baking assets of Defiance Mills for NZ$48 million. Page 26.

Christchurch scientists of Industrial Research Ltd are developing ultra-low temperature electronic devices. These will allow superconductor technology to provide clean power for large installations and lead to a new method of storing electrical energy. IRL in Wellington has been working on commercial applications for superconductor power transmission, with finance from ECNZ and in co-orporation with American Superconductor Corporation. Page 26.

Shortland Properties has increased its dividend on better earnings, and expects the property market to continue to improve in 1997. The Wellington-based property company on Tuesday reported a 55.4 percent higher bottom-line profit of $12.296 million in the year ended December 31. This compares with the 1995 profit of $7.912 million. Page 26.

Summit Gold NL expects to start drilling at its Carrick gold exploration project in Central Otago early in April. The first results were likely about a fortnight after drilling started, the managing director, Alan Eggers, said from Perth on Tuesday.

After failing to attract partners to the project early last year, Summit conducted soil sampling which threw up gold/arsenic anomalies similar to those at the producing Macraes field in east Otago. It is now getting approaches from other companies but is not looking for a partner. Page 26.
